answers.q1: A pass that edits the layout makes the built application depend on pass order and hides the layout's real content from its author, which is why passes may only read and report. When a pass throws, the runner turns the throw into a report of its own: an error with facts `[e]` and the fix "Passes are pure checks; guard reads that can be missing".
answers.q2: Because the rule is about a kit that is *absent*: if the finish kit is not installed, so is its pass, so nothing would ever check the layout. The running example therefore installs that one pass (framePass / CB-F102) on the shell instance, where it holds even when the kit is missing.
answers.q3: A stable code, a message, the call site in the layout, the facts that triggered it and a fix (the Structure table also lists the severity, warning or error).
answers.q4: When the rule is product policy that a layout may break on purpose, such as a finishing control in the Print module; breakage that cannot work, such as finish tools without the finish kit, is an error. Warnings let deliberate exceptions through, errors stop the build.

unclear: "Shell" is used four times (Solution, Structure, Collaborations, note 5) and never defined; a new reader cannot tell whether it is the application object, the `studio` in `.use(finishKit)`, or a layer above kits. Note 5's "shell instance" vs. the sketch's "shell pass" vs. `studio.use(...)` do not obviously name the same thing.

"Intermediate representation" is assumed from Chapter 10; the Solution never says what it actually contains (modules, regions, nodes) even though the sketch's pass walks `ir.modules` and `ir.find("viewport")`.

The ownership of contributed state and derived state is hand-waved: kits "contribute state … to the application under construction", but nothing says how keys are namespaced or what happens when two kits contribute the same name.
"Kits are named and versioned" is stated, but `requires ["core"]` carries no version constraint, and no behaviour is specified for a version mismatch.
"A reference to an uninstalled pass is a warning" (note 2) is cryptic: uninstalled where — a pass naming a pass in another kit, or a kit's `passes` list naming an absent pass?

How reports reach an agent is asserted (Collaborations: "shown to the layout author (and to the agent, for agent-written layouts)") but never described — machine-readable input, or only rendered text?

Whether passes run inside `build`/mount or as a separate command is only implied by the flowchart; Collaborations says build then run, the sketch puts `runPasses` at the end without saying who calls it.
errors: The claimed invariant "every report carries a code, a message, the call site, the facts and a fix" is violated by the chapter's own examples: `framePass` reports CB-F102 with no `at` and no `facts`, and `runPasses` reports `report(error, "cycle")` with neither message, facts nor fix.

The sketch's calling convention is inconsistent: `report(warning, "CB-F101", "…")` puts the code in slot 2, whereas `report(error, "cycle")` and `report(error, "pass threw", …)` put a *message* in that slot, contradicting "codes are stable" ("cycle" and "pass threw" are not CB codes).

The policy pass is implemented by string-matching (`module.label matches /print|darkroom/i`, `node.path starts with "finishing."`, `viewer.tools ∩ { crop, spot }`), which is exactly the brittle knowledge a central validator is said to lack. The IR apparently has no semantic module role or capability tag; the chapter should admit this and say the IR must carry roles, not labels.

The 'Clippy' known use is loose: Clippy ships with the Rust toolchain rather than being installed as a kit, and its allow/warn/deny levels are compiler lint levels configured by attributes and `clippy.toml`; it illustrates lint levels, not installable per-area rule bundles. (ESLint plugins, VS Code extensions and Blender add-ons are accurate.)

Note 7 admits the running example has no way to acknowledge a warning, yet the Consequences section claims warnings need acknowledgement 'or authors learn to ignore them' — the forces table's 'strict against helpful' tension is therefore unresolved in the worked example and should be flagged as such rather than listed as a settled benefit.
missing: No before/after example of an author actually repairing a reported layout, so the payoff ('precise, actionable reports') is asserted rather than shown.
No guidance on kit granularity: when does a domain area deserve its own kit rather than becoming a panel of another?
No codes for the installer's own failures; note 2 says a missing kit and a cycle each have their own code, but neither is named, while the two policy codes are.
No test story, although 'passes are another program to maintain, with their own tests' is a stated consequence; a one-line pattern (fixture IR → expected codes) would close it.
Nothing on how kit documentation is surfaced (help panel, agent context, layout comment expansion) despite note 8 making documentation part of the kit.
Nothing on incremental or repeated validation, although the Applicability section raises layouts built by user drags as a boundary case.
review.too_long: The single-paragraph Solution is overloaded — it states kits, dependency ordering, pass ordering, purity, report shape, severity semantics and the shell exception in one breath — and it overlaps Forces and notes 2, 4 and 5, which restate the same ordering, severity and shell rules; splitting Solution into three short paragraphs (kits, passes, reports) and deleting the duplication would shorten the chapter without losing a fact.
suggested_edits: Define 'shell' once, before the Solution, e.g. 'the studio instance that owns the viewport and installs kits (`studio.use(kit)`)'; then use the same word in note 5 and the sketch.

Replace the final Solution sentence with two sentences that state the shell exception and its reason: 'Some rules must hold when their kit is absent — a viewer listing the finish tools needs the finish kit. Install those passes on the studio instance, not in the kit.'

Fix the example reports so every one has code, severity, message, site, facts and fix (add `at: viewer.at, facts: [tool ids]` to CB-F102; give the cycle and thrown-pass reports real codes such as CB-F001/CB-F002).
Make the sketch's `report` signature explicit (`report(severity, code, message, at, facts, fix)`) so no reader has to infer argument order from two contradictory call styles.

Replace label regexes with IR facts the pass may legitimately read: give modules a `role` and tools a `capabilities` set, and match on those; note in Implementation notes that a pass reading `label` is a smell that the IR lacks the concept.
In note 5, add why kit-absent rules are a general obligation, not one special case: any negative rule ('never X here') that names a kit must be shell-installed, or the rule evaporates with the kit.
Trim or reframe the Clippy entry to 'Clippy demonstrates named lint groups with allow/warn/deny levels that code can override locally', or drop it for `dylint`-style third-party lint crates.

Add a short 'What a fix looks like' box: one report, then the one-line layout change that clears it, then the rebuilt mount — this also supports note 7's acknowledgement syntax (`// allow CB-F101: sampling a digital proof beside the enlarger`).

applications.context: An image editor where third-party and AI-powered tool packs (background removal, generative fill, upscaling, face retouching) are installed into user-arranged workspaces, and the product must guarantee that generative tools never appear in a 'forensic / documentary' workspace and always show provenance.

participants.Kit: A tool pack: `bgRemovalPack`, `generativeFillPack`, `upscalePack`, `faceRetouchPack`, `forensicPack`; each declares `requires`, contributes tool entries, commands, a panel, pack docs, and a *signed capability set* (e.g. `generative: true`, `emitsProvenance: true`).
participants.Kit installer: Workspace loader: resolves packs listed by the workspace document, orders them dependencies-first, refuses a missing pack or an unlicensed/absent model runtime, and reports dependency cycles.
participants.Tool: A single tool entry (e.g. 'generative fill' brush) with key, cursor, down/drag/up/hover/escape gestures, overlay (mask + preview) and an image override, plus its capability tag used by passes.
participants.Pass: `provenanceRequired` (a generative op must carry a provenance record) and `declaredCapabilitiesMatch` (a tool's runtime calls must be within its declared capabilities) — both pure functions over the built workspace IR.
participants.Pass runner: Runs before the workspace is mounted; orders passes by after/before, so the forensic and capability passes can read the results of an `indexTools` pass.
participants.Report: Code such as CB-G201, severity, message, the workspace-document call site (JSON pointer plus source line), facts (tool id, workspace role, provenance record), and a fix string the UI can render as 'Remove tool' or 'Change workspace role'.
participants.Shell-level pass: `noGenerativeInForensic` and `generativeToolNeedsPack`: they must fire precisely when the generative packs are *not* installed, or when a stale workspace references them, so they live on the application shell, not in any generative pack.

applications.sketch:
workspace "case-12-documentary":
  use(forensicPack)          // requires ["core", "provenance"]
  use(upscalePack)           // capabilities {generative: false}
  // generativeFill / faceRetouch deliberately not installed

shell pass generativeCapabilitiesIndexed on workspace after "slots":
  for tool in ir.allTools(): capabilities[tool.id] = tool.pack.capabilities   // facts others read

shell pass noGenerativeInForensic on workspace after "generativeCapabilitiesIndexed":
  for ws in ir.find("workspace") where ws.role == "forensic":
    for tool in ws.tools where capabilities[tool.id].generative:
      report(error, "CB-G201", "generative tool in a forensic workspace", at: tool.at,
             facts: [tool.id, "workspace role: forensic", capabilities[tool.id]],
             fix: "remove the tool, or change the workspace role to studio")

shell pass generativeToolNeedsPack on workspace after "generativeCapabilitiesIndexed":
  for tool in ir.allTools() where capabilities[tool.id].generative and not installed(tool.pack):
    report(error, "CB-G202", "workspace lists a generative tool whose pack is not installed", at: tool.at,
           facts: [tool.id, tool.pack], fix: ".use(generativeFillPack) or remove the tool")

pack pass provenanceRequired on ops after "generativeCapabilitiesIndexed":
  for op in ir.ops where capabilities[op.toolId].generative and op.provenance == none:
    report(error, "CB-G203", "generative result without provenance", at: op.at,
           facts: [op.id, op.modelId, "prompt+seed+source hash missing"],
           fix: "attach a provenance record; the export writes it into the sidecar")

build(ws): installPacks(ws.packs) -> buildIR -> runPasses -> mount only if no errors
applications.key_note: Implementation note 5, 'some rules belong to the shell, not the kit': the guarantee is a *negative* rule about generative tools, and a negative rule whose enforcement is shipped inside the thing it forbids disappears exactly when the thing is absent — a documentary build will not have generativeFillPack installed, so only a shell pass can still catch a stale workspace and, more importantly, nobody can uninstall the guard. Note 4 follows from it: CB-G201 and CB-G202 are breakage (error), while a 'provisional export' or 'evidence copy' policy would be a warn-level policy with an explicit allow.
applications.failure_or_adaptation: Two adaptations are required. First, workspace layout here is *user-arranged and dragged*, so the build step the pattern assumes (Applicability's third bullet) has to become a validate-on-every-change loop, and warnings need the acknowledgement mechanism note 7 admits the running example lacks — otherwise users learn to ignore the badge. Second, capability declarations are static but AI tools are not: a third-party 'enhance' pack can call generative fill behind an innocent declaration, and a model upgrade can change behaviour after the pass ran, so build-time passes must be paired with runtime enforcement (provenance written at generation time, capability checks on the model call) and with signature/verification of third-party packs. Purely static checking cannot deliver 'never appears' on its own.

applications.context: A node-based colour-grading application where a 'film emulation' pack must enforce that its nodes come after the input colour-space transform and before the output transform, and where an assistant agent can author new node layouts.

participants.Kit: `filmEmulationPack` v2: node types (halation, grain, print tone curve), a node-menu contribution, a parameter panel, pack state, docs stating the colour-space rule, and the `filamentOrderPass`; `requires: ["colorspace"]`.
participants.Kit installer: Graph layout loader: orders packs dependencies-first so the colour-space pack is installed before film emulation; a graph authoring raw node ids without the pack installed, or a requires cycle, is a report.
participants.Tool: The authoring affordance: an 'insert film emulation' menu/gesture, the drag handle on a film node, a node-graph overlay showing the IDT/ODT boundaries, key `F`.
participants.Pass: `filamentOrderPass` over the graph IR: for each node contributed by the pack, check IDT ∈ upstream and ODT ∉ downstream, and report per offending node.
participants.Pass runner: Orders `graphTopology` (which precomputes upstream/downstream sets) before `filamentOrderPass`; converts a throwing pass into an error with the 'guard reads that can be missing' fix (graphs authored by agents are frequently malformed or cyclic).
participants.Report: CB-C301/CB-C302 with the node's call site in the agent-authored layout, facts naming the offending node and the transform it violates, and a fix string the agent can apply as a graph edit.
participants.Shell-level pass: `filmNodesNeedPack` (a graph contains halation/grain/tonePrint ids but the pack is not installed or licensed) and a shell-level 'unguarded film emulation' rule, both installed on the shell so they survive the pack's absence.

applications.sketch:
pack filmEmulation v2:
  requires ["colorspace"]
  nodes: halation, grain, tonePrint
  passes: [filamentOrderPass]          // after graphTopology
  docs: "film emulation is scene-referred: after the IDT, before the ODT"
  returns: { nodeMenu, filmPanel, keys }

pass graphTopology on graph after "slots":
  upstream := reachability over incoming edges; downstream := over outgoing edges

pass filamentOrderPass on graph after "graphTopology":
  idt := ir.nodeOfType("inputTransform"); odt := ir.nodeOfType("outputTransform")
  for n in ir.nodes where n.packId == "filmEmulation":
    if idt not in upstream(n):
      report(error, "CB-C301", "film emulation is upstream of the input transform", at: n.at,
             facts: [n.id, idt.id], fix: "move the node after the input colour-space transform")
    if odt in downstream(n):
      report(error, "CB-C302", "film emulation is downstream of the output transform", at: n.at,
             facts: [n.id, odt.id], fix: "move the node before the output transform")

shell pass filmNodesNeedPack on graph after "slots":
  for n in ir.nodes where n.type in {halation, grain, tonePrint} and not installed("filmEmulation"):
    report(error, "CB-C303", "graph uses film emulation nodes without the pack", at: n.at,
           facts: [n.id], fix: ".use(filmEmulationPack)")

-- agent loop: layout := agent.author(); rs := runPasses(layout); agent.apply(rs.fixes); rebuild
applications.key_note: Implementation note 1, passes are pure — with note 3's shared refusal shape doing double duty. An assistant agent authors the graph, so any pass that *fixes* placement silently makes the rendered result depend on pass order and hides the graph's real content from both the agent and the human reviewing it: the agent would keep regenerating the same mis-ordered layout while the image looked right. The pattern therefore demands the repair be returned as data (the 'fixing passes' variation) in the same code/facts/fix shape the pipeline refuses ill-typed graphs with (Chapter 5), so a machine can apply it and a person can read it.
applications.failure_or_adaptation: Placement in a DAG is not node-local in the way a module slot is: a film node downstream of a *merge* may sit after the IDT on one path and before it on another, so the rule needs an explicit definition ('every path from source to the node passes through the IDT' for the first check; 'no path from the node reaches the ODT without...' for the second) and the chapter's simple `framePass`-style walk is not enough — reachability must be a separate, declared-before pass. Graphs also churn on every node drag, so the run must be incremental rather than build-time-only, and agent-authored graphs will contain cycles and dangling references, which is exactly the case note 1's 'guard reads that can be missing' fix anticipates. Finally, node *group* and nested-composition boundaries, plus metadata-driven colour-space switches that only resolve at render time, escape a static IR check and need a runtime guard.
